title: How a program asks the kernel for something
objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe what happens between calling write() in C and the kernel running, explain why syscall numbers differ between architectures, and say why some 'system calls' never enter the kernel at all.

blocks.text: In your C source, write(fd, buf, n) looks exactly like any other function call. It is not one. It is a request handed across the boundary from the previous lesson, and the machinery that carries it is worth understanding — because it explains performance, it explains errno, and it explains what a tool like strace is showing you.

rows: An ordinary C function call into the C library
Puts the arguments in the right registers, executes the syscall instruction, translates the result
Looks up the number in its table, validates, does the work, returns a value

blocks.text: The C library is a thin translator here, not a decision-maker. Its job is to know the calling convention: which register holds the call number, which hold the arguments, what the instruction is on this processor, and how the kernel's return value maps onto the C convention of returning -1 and setting errno.

blocks.caption: The same request at two levels
lines: /* Through the library — portable, this is what you normally write */
/* The same request, naming the call by number yourself */
/* SYS_write is a constant from the headers, not a universal value. */

blocks.text: The numbers are per-architecture, and that matters

Every system call has a number, and the kernel uses it as an index into a table. Those numbers are part of the architecture's ABI, not a Linux-wide constant. The same call has a different number on a 64-bit Intel machine than on a 64-bit ARM machine — and some calls do not exist at all on the newer one.

blocks.title: Why aarch64 has no open() and no fork()
blocks.text: aarch64 was defined long after those calls had better replacements, so it shipped only the modern ones: openat() takes a directory descriptor plus a path and can therefore express 'relative to this directory' safely, and clone() covers everything fork() did plus threads. On ARM your program still calls open() and fork() in C — the library translates them into openat() and clone(). This is why you should never hardcode a syscall number, and why strace output can look unfamiliar on a different machine.

The kernel does not have errno. It returns a single value: a small negative number means failure and encodes which failure. The library checks for that range, stores the positive equivalent in errno, and returns -1 to you. That is the whole mechanism behind the pattern you already use.

blocks.caption: What the wrapper does on your behalf
lines: perror("open");        /* open: No such file or directory */
/* the kernel returned -2; the wrapper set errno = 2 (ENOENT) and returned -1 */
/* Which is why errno is only meaningful after a call that FAILED. */
/* A successful call may leave any value there. */

blocks.text: Some calls never enter the kernel

Reading the clock is requested constantly by almost every program. Crossing the boundary for it would be an enormous, pointless tax — so Linux maps a small page of kernel-provided code into every process, called the vDSO. Calls like clock_gettime() run that code in user mode, reading a shared time page, and return without ever crossing.

blocks.title: You can measure the difference yourself
blocks.text: On one aarch64 machine, clock_gettime through the vDSO took about 27 ns per call while the same call forced through the real syscall path took about 298 ns — roughly eleven times slower. Your numbers will differ; the ratio is the point, and the exercise below has you measure it on your own machine rather than trusting anyone's figure.

blocks.title: Watch and time the boundary
steps: Run: strace -c cat /etc/hostname            (a count of every call, grouped)
Read that output as a story: find the library being loaded, then the file, then the write to the screen
Run: grep -E 'vdso|vvar' /proc/self/maps    (the kernel's code mapped into you)
Run: strace -e trace=clock_gettime date     (notice how few, or none, appear — that is the vDSO)
Run: strace -c dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null bs=1 count=20000 2>&1 | tail -6
Run: strace -c dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null bs=20000 count=1 2>&1 | tail -6
blocks.expected: The two dd runs move identical bytes; the call counts differ by four orders of magnitude. And the clock_gettime trace shows almost nothing, because that call is answered without a crossing at all — the two facts together are the practical summary of this lesson.

cheatsheet: write() in C is a library wrapper, not the system call itself
The wrapper loads registers, executes the syscall instruction, and translates the result
Every call has a number that indexes the kernel's table
Numbers are per-architecture: write is 1 on x86-64 and 64 on aarch64
aarch64 has no open() or fork() — libc maps them to openat() and clone()
Never hardcode a syscall number; use the SYS_* constants
The kernel returns a small negative value on error; the wrapper sets errno and returns -1
errno is only meaningful after a call that failed
The vDSO answers clock calls in user mode with no crossing at all
strace -c counts calls; strace -e trace=... shows the sequence

checkpoint.prompt: Where does errno actually get set?

choices.A: It is read from /proc after each call
choices.B: The CPU sets it in a status register
choices.C: The kernel writes it into your process
choices.D: The C library wrapper sets it after seeing a negative return value from the kernel

checkpoint.explanation: The kernel returns one value and encodes failure as a small negative number. Translating that into -1 plus errno is entirely the library's work — which is why errno only means anything after a failure.

checkpoint.prompt: Your code calls open() and it works on both x86-64 and aarch64, yet aarch64 has no open syscall. How?

choices.A: open() is a macro that becomes a file read
choices.B: aarch64 kernels add it at boot
choices.C: The kernel emulates the missing call
choices.D: The C library implements open() using the openat() syscall on that architecture

checkpoint.explanation: This is exactly the job of the wrapper layer: a stable C interface on top of whatever the architecture's ABI actually provides. Hardcoding a syscall number throws that portability away.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does calling clock_gettime() in a tight loop cost far less than calling getpid() in the same loop?

choices.A: The C library caches the time
choices.B: clock_gettime is answered by vDSO code running in user mode, with no boundary crossing

checkpoint.explanation: The vDSO is kernel-provided code mapped into your address space. The clock is read from a shared page in user mode, so the expensive part — the crossing — never happens.

checkpoint.prompt: You want to know which system calls a misbehaving program is making. What is the first tool to reach for?

choices.A: Reading the kernel source for the syscall table
choices.B: gdb, stepping through instruction by instruction
choices.D: strace, which reports every call, its arguments, and its result

checkpoint.explanation: strace shows the whole conversation between the program and the kernel, including the failing call and its errno — usually before you need a debugger at all.
